title: Centralised identity-holder breaches
description: Documented large-scale breaches at centralised holders of identity data (credit bureaus, national ID databases, large identity providers) show that a single recognised certifier concentrating everyone's data is a single point of compromise affecting people who never chose that provider.
source: Public breach disclosures and regulator reports on centralised identity/credit data breaches; specific incidents to be attached via attach_source.

title: Existing graded assurance frameworks
description: eIDAS defines levels of assurance (low/substantial/high) and member-state trusted lists of supervised providers; NIST SP 800-63 defines identity/authenticator/federation assurance levels and expects the relying party to choose required levels by its own risk assessment. This shows that public grading scales and relying-party-chosen minimums already exist, which both supports the feasibility of grading and weakens the novelty claim.
source: The eIDAS regulation and implementing acts on assurance levels and trusted lists; NIST SP 800-63 digital identity guidelines. Exact editions/sections to be attached via attach_source.

provenance.quote: Assurance levels low, substantial and high for electronic identification means issued under a notified electronic identification scheme shall be determined with reference to the specifications and procedures set out in the Annex.

title: Insurance-backed liability for trust providers already required
description: Qualified trust service providers under eIDAS are required to maintain sufficient financial resources or liability insurance to cover damages from their services, and commercial identity-certification schemes (e.g. Osmio-style) similarly tie certification to a liable, insured certifier. This supports feasibility of per-certifier insured liability but shows it is prior art.
source: eIDAS provisions on QTSP liability and financial resources; public descriptions of Osmio's certification model. To be verified and attached via attach_source.

provenance.quote: Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS): Article 13 sets liability of trust service providers; Article 24(2)(c) requires qualified trust service providers to maintain sufficient financial resources and/or obtain appropriate liability insurance.

title: Car-share and P2P platforms already buy per-check identity verification
description: Peer-to-peer car-sharing and mobility platforms already pay third-party verification vendors per customer check and rely on third-party insurance for theft and damage, and report fraud losses from synthetic identities. This shows a relying party with an existing budget and a motive to accept more verified strangers, supporting buildability.
source: Industry descriptions of verification and insurance arrangements by car-sharing platforms and their vendors; fraud-loss statements. To be attached via attach_source.

title: eIDAS trust-service regime: plural qualified providers with liability and insurance
description: The EU eIDAS framework establishes member-state trusted lists of qualified trust service providers (QTSPs), assigns them liability for damage caused by failure to meet obligations, and requires financial capacity (typically insurance) to cover that liability — without a shared cross-provider store of personal data. This shows the liable, insured, plural-certifier model is legally and commercially operable, though liability there attaches to the trust service, not explicitly to per-check identity outcomes.
source: EU eIDAS regulation and its implementing trusted-list regime, as generally described in public regulatory summaries; specific articles not consulted here and must be attached via attach_source.

title: NIST SP 800-63 identity assurance levels tier checks by inputs and process
description: NIST's digital identity guidelines define identity assurance levels (IAL1–3) distinguished by what evidence was collected, how it was validated, and whether proofing was remote or in person. This demonstrates that a public, input-based scale of check thoroughness is a well-understood, already-published construct — which both supports the feasibility of a grading scale and raises the prior-art question of whether a new one is needed.
source: NIST Special Publication 800-63 series (Digital Identity Guidelines), known from general familiarity; the exact revision and sections were not consulted for this graph.

title: Hashed-lookup and revocation-flag designs in deployed privacy-preserving systems
description: Deployed systems use hashed or k-anonymised lookups to check whether a value (e.g., a compromised password, a revoked certificate serial) appears on a list without disclosing the value or attributes about it. Certificate revocation lists and status-list credentials carry a document-level 'revoked' bit with no reason or attributes. These are the kind of mechanism the minimal fraud signal relies on; they also illustrate the known weakness that low-entropy inputs (document numbers) can be dictionary-attacked and that query patterns can leak unless the lookup is designed to prevent it.
source: General knowledge of breached-password range-query services, X.509 CRL/OCSP, and W3C-style status-list credential designs; no specific specification consulted for this graph.

title: Industry reports of synthetic and stolen-identity fraud in vehicle rental and car-sharing
description: Mobility and rental operators report that vehicle theft via fraudulent bookings is commonly executed with stolen or synthetic identities and forged driving licences, and that operators relying on in-house document checks or closed member networks either lose vehicles or reject legitimate out-of-network customers. This is the kind of evidence that establishes the problem the thesis addresses and the cost of options (1) and (2).
source: Trade-press and operator statements on car-share/rental identity fraud, described from general familiarity; a specific report should be attached via attach_source before this is relied on.
